## Score Descriptions:

### Vulnerability:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Vulnerability on the Northeast Shelf for Cobia"
#| label: fig-vuln
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean Vulnerability within Cobia’s range on the Northeast Shelf was **Low** (2.17 +/- 0.91) (@fig-sum-tab). This was consistent across the species range in the region (@fig-vuln). Vulnerability was also Low when exposures were calculated using only factors that were important to species distributions (@fig-sum-tab).

Cobia were given a High Vulnerability score in the recent assessment on the Southeast Shelf [@burton2023climate].

### Climate Exposure:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/total_exposure_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Exposure on the Northeast Shelf for Cobia"
#| label: fig-exp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/total_exposure_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean Exposure within Cobia’s range on the Northeast Shelf was Moderate (2.17 +/- 0.91) (@fig-sum-tab). Exposure was greatest along the coasts of Delaware, Maryland, North Carolina, and in the mouth of the Delaware Bay. They were lowest at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay (@fig-exp). These patterns were driven by high surface salinity and pH exposures (@fig-fact-exp).

Cobia was not assessed in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Northeast Shelf, but was assessed in the recent assessment for the Southeast Shelf. In this assessment, Cobia received a Very High exposure score, driven by sea surface temperature, salinity and ocean acidificiation [@burton2023climate].

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| label: fig-exp-imp

knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/total_exposure_map_timeseries_imp", ext)))
```

Cobia distributions in the region were driven by sea surface temperature and mixed layer depth. Cobia prefer warmer waters [@crear2020contemporary]. These two variables did not have high exposures within the species range, and as a result, exposure was Low (1.05 +/- 0.25) when exposure was calculated only with these factors (@fig-sum-tab).

### Biological Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/sensitivity_map", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Cobia/sensitivity_map", ext)))
```

Cobia received a **Low** sensitivity score. Certainty was 53% (@fig-sum-tab). The only attribute that received a score greater than 2.5 was Relationship to Calcified Organisms (@fig-sum-tab). Cobia primarily consume crustaceans, which make them vulnerable to ocean acidification [@smith1995life].

Cobia was not assessed in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Northeast Shelf, but was assessed in the recent assessment for the Southeast Shelf. In this assessment, it received a Moderate sensitivity score. This score was driven by Dispersal of Early Life Stages, Early Life History Survival and Settlement Requirements, Reproductive Complexity, Spawning Cycle, and Sensitivity to Ocean Acidification [@burton2023climate].

### Directional Effect:

Experts predicted that climate change would have a **neutral** effect on Cobia. Certainty was 95%. Warmer temperatures could lead to northward shifts in distributions and earlier seasonal migrations [@crear2020contemporary]. The recent Southeast US Climate Vulnerability Assessment also predicted that climate change would have a neutral effect on Cobia [@burton2023climate].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

Cobia off the eastern U.S. Atlantic coast currently overwinter offshore in waters south of North Carolina. Suitable habitat increases in the summer months with warming temperatures. Habitat distribution models suggest increased habitat suitability northward, shifting distributions poleward, and possible earlier seasonal migrations [@crear2020contemporary]. This shift northward could prompt revision of management regulations as the fishery expands to new states or regions. Early life stage cobia may be somewhat resistant to projected rises in CO^2^ levels [@ebanks2013influence], although juvenile cobia in a laboratory study exhibited poor growth performance and reduced feeding at elevated temperatures [@le2024impact]. 

## Life History Synopsis

Cobia are a pelagic, continental shelf fish distributed from Massachusetts to Argentina but are most abundant from Virginia to the Gulf of America [@shaffer1989synopsis]. Two stocks are recognized in the United States: one along the Atlantic coast south to Georgia and the other along the Atlantic coast of Florida into the Gulf [@sedar2020sedar58]. Cobia are batch spawners, and move inshore to spawn when temperatures reach 20-25°C. They spawn over a period of 4-6 weeks, peaking in June-July in Virginia [@joseph1964spawning]. Cobia eggs hatch within 36 hours of fertilization. Given the short time frame between fertilization and hatching, it is likely that eggs and larvae do not travel far from spawning grounds [@shaffer1989synopsis]. Little is known about the feeding habits of larval and juvenile cobia. Adult cobia are generalist carnivores, feeding on benthic-epibenthic crustaceans (*Portunids* and *Callinectes* sp.), teleosts, cephalopods, and elasmobranchs [@smith1995life]. Juveniles are pelagic and often associated with structure for feeding and shelter. Juveniles and adults can be found near shipwrecks, buoys, shellfish beds, and submerged aquatic vegetation [@sedar2020sedar58]. Few predators of cobia in U.S. Atlantic waters are known, although dolphinfish (*Coryphaena hippurus*) have been reported to prey on small cobia [@shaffer1989synopsis]. Over 50% of cobia are mature by age 2, and can live up to 15 years [@sedar2020sedar58]. Adults are highly migratory. Cobia exhibit a general migratory trend of overwintering in south Florida and the Florida Keys waters, and then migrating north along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts in late winter-early spring.  They likely return to south Florida coastal waters in the late fall [@hendon2008seasonal]. The Atlantic migratory cobia are managed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission. The population is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring as of the last benchmark stock assessment in 2020 [@sedar2020sedar58].
